passages.text: Rong Zongjing moved to Shanghai at fourteen to apprentice at a native bank, then in 1896 started his own native bank with his father and brother before pivoting into flour milling and textiles in 1902.

Rong Zongjing articulated an expansionist posture toward capital and industrial capacity, indicating a willingness to take on borrowing to fund acquisition and to absorb any factory offered for sale — a stance that powered the Rong family's rapid horizontal integration across early-20th-century Chinese industry.

By 1921 the Rong brothers' 14 flour mills produced about 250,000 kilograms of flour daily -- roughly a third of China's total flour output -- while their cotton factories accounted for about 30 percent of national cotton output.
Opened a small flour mill in Wuxi in 1902 using profits from the brothers' native bank, marking the pivot from finance into industrial manufacturing.
The single Wuxi flour mill grew into a national flour-and-textile empire; by 1938 (Rong Zongjing's death) the business was among the largest private domestic enterprises in China.
Expanded rapidly through debt-financed acquisition of additional flour and textile mills through the 1900s-1920s.
By 1921 the combined flour and textile operations held roughly one-third of national flour output and 30 percent of cotton output, per Global Times.

Rong Zongjing — founder profiled in the Chinese Founder Ledger — is documented as follows: wuxi-born industrialist who, with younger brother Rong Desheng, built China's largest privately owned flour-milling and cotton-textile empire in the Republican era, reportedly controlling roughly a third of China's flour output and 30 percent of its cotton output by the early 1920s. The profile is grounded in the 2 sources indexed for this founder.

Rong Zongjing's role is documented as: co-founder and elder-brother lead of the Rong flour-and-textile business empire; primarily drove business expansion Deceased 1938, per Wikipedia (research date: 2026-08-23).

Rong-zongjing belongs to Group 1 - Pre-1949 pioneers. The pre-1949 pioneers group anchors the ledger in China's early industrial modernization, covering founders who built flour, textile, match, and cotton-mill enterprises in the late-Qing and Republican periods, before the 1949 establishment of the People's Republic reshaped private industry.
